quests.correctSentence: English is spoken in many countries.
quests.contrastSentence: English are spoken in many countries.
quests.ruleExplanation: Passive voice (is/are + past participle) shifts focus to the receiver of the action: English is spoken. 'English' is singular, so it takes 'is'.
quests.nativeTip: The focus here is on the language being spoken, not on who speaks it.

quests.correctSentence: These cars are made in Japan.
quests.contrastSentence: These cars is made in Japan.
quests.ruleExplanation: Plural subjects take 'are' in present simple passive: cars are made. The focus is on where the cars come from, not who makes them.
quests.nativeTip: The subject 'these cars' is plural.

quests.correctSentence: — How is this bread made? — It is baked fresh every morning.
quests.contrastSentence: — How is this bread made? — It are baked fresh every morning.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Is baked' describes a regular routine in present simple passive: it is baked every morning, matching the question's own tense.
quests.nativeTip: This describes a regular routine happening now, in general.

quests.correctSentence: The letter was sent yesterday.
quests.contrastSentence: The letter is sent yesterday.
quests.ruleExplanation: Past simple passive uses 'was' for singular subjects: the letter was sent yesterday. 'Is' would wrongly place this in the present.
quests.nativeTip: 'Yesterday' places this action in the past, and the subject is singular.

quests.correctSentence: The windows were broken during the storm.
quests.contrastSentence: The windows was broken during the storm.
quests.ruleExplanation: Plural subjects take 'were' in past simple passive: windows were broken. This matches the past time reference 'during the storm'.
quests.nativeTip: The subject 'windows' is plural, and the storm is in the past.

quests.correctSentence: — Who painted this? — It was painted by a famous artist.
quests.contrastSentence: — Who painted this? — It is painted by a famous artist.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Was painted' places the action in the past, appropriate for describing an existing painting's history.
quests.nativeTip: The painting happened at some point in the past.

quests.correctSentence: The road is being repaired right now.
quests.contrastSentence: The road are being repaired right now.
quests.ruleExplanation: Present continuous passive (is/are + being + past participle) describes an action happening now: the road is being repaired.
quests.nativeTip: 'Right now' signals an action in progress, and the subject is singular.

quests.correctSentence: New houses are being built in this area.
quests.contrastSentence: New houses is being built in this area.
quests.ruleExplanation: Plural subjects take 'are' in present continuous passive: houses are being built, an ongoing process happening currently.
quests.nativeTip: The subject 'houses' is plural, and this is ongoing right now.

quests.correctSentence: — Why is it so noisy outside? — The bridge is being fixed.
quests.contrastSentence: — Why is it so noisy outside? — The bridge were being fixed.
quests.ruleExplanation: The ongoing noise points to present continuous passive: is being fixed right now, matching the pattern from Question 1.
quests.nativeTip: The noise suggests something is happening at this very moment.

quests.correctSentence: The report has been finished.
quests.contrastSentence: The report have been finished.
quests.ruleExplanation: Present perfect passive (has/have + been + past participle) connects a completed action to now: the report has been finished.
quests.nativeTip: This connects a completed action to the present, and the subject is singular.

quests.correctSentence: All the tickets have been sold.
quests.contrastSentence: All the tickets has been sold.
quests.ruleExplanation: Plural subjects take 'have' in present perfect passive: tickets have been sold, a result relevant right now.
quests.nativeTip: The subject 'tickets' is plural.

quests.correctSentence: — Is the package here yet? — Yes, it has been delivered.
quests.contrastSentence: — Is the package here yet? — Yes, it had been delivered.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Yet' commonly pairs with present perfect: has been delivered, connecting the delivery to the present moment, matching Question 1.
quests.nativeTip: The question word 'yet' is a classic signal for this present-focused tense.

quests.correctSentence: This form must be completed in black ink.
quests.contrastSentence: This form must is completed in black ink.
quests.ruleExplanation: Modals combine with passive voice as 'modal + be + past participle': must be completed. After any modal, the verb stays in its base form, so 'be' fits, not 'is' or 'being'.
quests.nativeTip: After a modal like 'must', the verb needs its base form.

quests.correctSentence: The task can be finished by Friday.
quests.contrastSentence: The task can is finished by Friday.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Can' also needs 'be' before the past participle: can be finished, following the same modal passive pattern from Question 1.
quests.nativeTip: The same base-form rule after modals applies here too.

quests.correctSentence: — When will the decision be made? — It should be made by next week.
quests.contrastSentence: — When will the decision be made? — It should is made by next week.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Should' also requires 'be' before the past participle: should be made, continuing the same modal passive pattern throughout this level.
quests.nativeTip: 'Should' is a modal, so this follows the same rule as Questions 1 and 2.

quests.correctSentence: My car was stolen last night, and I have no idea who did it.
quests.contrastSentence: My car stole last night, and I have no idea who did it.
quests.ruleExplanation: Passive voice fits perfectly when the agent is unknown: my car was stolen, and I don't know who did it. Active voice would require naming who stole it.
quests.nativeTip: The person responsible is completely unknown here.

quests.correctSentence: The chef prepared this dish personally, using his grandmother's recipe.
quests.contrastSentence: The chef was prepared this dish personally, using his grandmother's recipe.
quests.ruleExplanation: Active voice fits when the agent (the chef) is important and known: the chef prepared this dish. This contrasts with Question 1, where the agent was unknown.
quests.nativeTip: The chef, the person doing the action, is the clear focus and star of this sentence.

quests.correctSentence: — Who broke the vase? — It's not clear; it was broken somehow.
quests.contrastSentence: — Who broke the vase? — It's not clear; it broke somehow.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since the responsible person is unclear, passive voice fits: it was broken somehow, focusing on the vase rather than an unknown culprit.
quests.nativeTip: Nobody knows who is responsible, just like the stolen car in Question 1.

quests.correctSentence: The novel was written by a famous author.
quests.contrastSentence: The novel was written from a famous author.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'By' introduces the agent in passive voice when it's worth mentioning: written by a famous author.
quests.nativeTip: This preposition introduces the person who performed the action in a passive sentence.

quests.equation: Key Form: The window was broken.
quests.correctSentence: Which sentence correctly omits the agent because it's unknown or unimportant?
quests.contrastSentence: Which sentence correctly omits the agent because it's unknown or unimportant?
quests.ruleExplanation: When the agent is unknown or unimportant, passive voice simply drops the 'by' phrase entirely: the window was broken. Saying 'by someone' is grammatically fine but unnecessary here.
quests.nativeTip: When the agent doesn't matter, the 'by' phrase is often dropped entirely.

quests.correctSentence: — Who fixed your computer? — It was fixed by a technician from the shop.
quests.contrastSentence: — Who fixed your computer? — It was fixed from a technician from the shop.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since the question asks specifically who did it, mentioning the agent with 'by' is appropriate: fixed by a technician.
quests.nativeTip: Since the question specifically asks 'who', naming the agent here makes sense.

quests.correctSentence: The new bridge will be completed next year.
quests.contrastSentence: The new bridge is completed next year.
quests.ruleExplanation: Future passive (will be + past participle) describes future events: the bridge will be completed next year.
quests.nativeTip: 'Next year' points to a future event, not something already finished.

quests.correctSentence: The results will be announced next Monday.
quests.contrastSentence: The results will announced next Monday.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Will be announced' fits this future event, matching the pattern from Question 1: will be announced next Monday.
quests.nativeTip: 'Next Monday' signals another future event.

quests.correctSentence: — When will we hear back? — You will be notified by email.
quests.contrastSentence: — When will we hear back? — You are notified by email.
quests.ruleExplanation: The future question 'when will we hear back' calls for future passive in the answer: you will be notified, matching Questions 1 and 2.
quests.nativeTip: The question about the future signals what tense the answer should use.

quests.correctSentence: This building was built in 1990.
quests.contrastSentence: This building is built in 1990.
quests.ruleExplanation: A specific past year calls for past simple passive: was built in 1990, reviewing the pattern from Level 142.
quests.nativeTip: '1990' is a specific finished point in the past.

quests.correctSentence: The email has already been sent.
quests.contrastSentence: The email had already been sent.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Already' pairs with present perfect passive: has already been sent, reviewing the pattern from Level 144.
quests.nativeTip: 'Already' signals a result connected to the present moment.

quests.correctSentence: — Is dinner ready? — Almost, it is being prepared now.
quests.contrastSentence: — Is dinner ready? — Almost, it was being prepared now.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Now' calls for present continuous passive: is being prepared, reviewing the pattern from Level 143.
quests.nativeTip: 'Now' signals an action in progress at this exact moment.

quests.correctSentence: Visitors are requested to sign in at the front desk.
quests.contrastSentence: Visitors was requested to sign in at the front desk.
quests.ruleExplanation: This is a general present-tense rule, and 'visitors' is plural, so 'are requested' fits: a very common wording for official notices.
quests.nativeTip: This is a general, standing rule for a plural group of people.

quests.correctSentence: Local school was awarded a grant for new technology.
quests.contrastSentence: Local school is awarded a grant for new technology.
quests.ruleExplanation: News reports typically describe completed events in past simple passive: was awarded a grant, a common structure in headlines and articles.
quests.nativeTip: News headlines usually report a completed past event.

quests.correctSentence: — Has the new policy been announced? — Yes, it was announced this morning.
quests.contrastSentence: — Has the new policy been announced? — Yes, it is announced this morning.
quests.ruleExplanation: Even though the question used present perfect, the specific time 'this morning' calls for past simple in the answer: was announced this morning, closing out Stage 8's opening block on passive voice.
quests.nativeTip: 'This morning' is a specific finished time, even though the question used present perfect.
